source.title: Bayesian Deep Learning and a Probabilistic Perspective of Generalization

record.tranche_reason: The study measures test error across ResNet-18 widths and refines the double-descent result by showing that its shape depends on the inference method: it appears with SGD, is reduced with SWAG, and is mitigated with MultiSWAG.
record.gate_note: The authors also discuss double descent in related work and cite other studies; those cited results are not recorded as rows. Rows below are from the study's own width sweeps. Numerical curve values are shown only in figures, while the text gives qualitative descriptions.
record.test_reason: The study reruns the Nakkiran et al. ResNet-18 width sweep on CIFAR-100 with SGD and reproduces model-wise double descent. It then shows the curve depends on the predictor: SWAG reduces the peak, and MultiSWAG (and, per the text, deep ensembles) removes it. This is a specific result that V1 needs restating for marginalized or ensembled predictors, so T5. It also compares clean labels with 10% and 20% label noise, which bears on V6's noise dependence.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that SGD-trained ResNet-18s show model-wise double descent, especially under label noise. SWAG reduces it, though it clearly persists at 20% noise. MultiSWAG, and similarly deep ensembles, remove it entirely, giving monotonic improvement with width in both error and NLL. They present this as predicted by their view that Bayesian model averaging with reasonable priors should improve monotonically with flexibility.
record.recipe_differences: The study follows the ResNet-18 width-sweep setup described as following Nakkiran et al. (2019), but adds comparisons among SGD, SWAG, and MultiSWAG rather than reproducing only the original method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported double-descent behavior changes with inference/training method (SGD, SWAG, MultiSWAG) and with label corruption (original labels, 10%, 20%).

fits_no_version.finding: Test NLL versus width follows the same method-dependent pattern as error. SGD shows double descent, SWAG reduces it, and MultiSWAG shows none.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-wise double descent in test NLL (loss rather than error) for ResNet-18 depends on the inference method and is removed by multi-basin Bayesian model averaging.

record.problems: The double-descent values are presented in figures without numerical curve values or reported uncertainty. The width-sweep evidence is limited to ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100.

untested.parts: Only ResNet-18 width on CIFAR-100 is tested. No other architectures or datasets. The interpolation threshold location is not identified or tied to the peak.
No non-deep model classes are swept for double descent.
No effective-complexity measure is computed or used to predict peak location.
Multiple peaks are not studied, nor is variance as a separate driver. The claim that optimally tuned regularization removes the peak is only cited (Nakkiran et al. 2020), not tested.
The authors argue that parameter counting is a poor proxy for complexity. They do not re-express the curve against an effective parameter count.

missing.what: Deep ensembles also mitigate double descent in the 20% noise error sweep, with about 1–2% worse accuracy than MultiSWAG. This is stated in the text only.

MultiSWAG test error (and NLL) as the number of independent SWAG models varies (1, 3, 5, 10) at 20% noise. Double descent is alleviated as the number of modes grows, so the count of averaged modes controls the peak.

record.verdict_notes: All double-descent evidence is figure-only, with no numbers or uncertainty, so states rest on the authors' qualitative wording. The SGD arm is a near-replication of Nakkiran et al.'s width sweep, which is not an original source here. The MultiSWAG arms compare ensembles of 100–200 networks against single networks, so 'model size' refers to member width, not total predictor size. NLL rows are kept off V1 because V1 names test error. V7 is only discussed: the authors argue that parameter counting is a poor proxy, but they do not test it.

versions.untested_parts: Only ResNet-18 width sweeps on CIFAR-100 are tested; other architectures, datasets, and training procedures are not tested.
Changing training sample size near the interpolation threshold.
Double descent across model classes beyond the tested neural networks.
Whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.

The width-sweep results compare uncorrupted labels with 10% and 20% label corruption. They do not test multiple peaks, variance as a separate source, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The study does not re-express complexity using an effective parameter count or show that this turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.condition: MultiSWAG (multi-basin averaging over 5–10 SWAG models); text also reports deep ensembles
relationships.reason: Test error decreases monotonically with width and no peak appears (r7, r8, r9). Double descent therefore holds for single-solution predictors, not for these ensembled or marginalized ones. Labelled limits_scope rather than challenges because V1 concerns ordinarily trained networks.
relationships.display_finding: MultiSWAG averaging 5–10 SWAG models and deep ensembles produced monotonically decreasing test error with width, without a peak.

relationships.condition: SWAG and MultiSWAG under 10%/20% label noise
relationships.reason: With label noise held fixed, the peak shrinks under SWAG (r5, r6) and vanishes under MultiSWAG (r8, r9). So noise produces the peak only for point-estimate or single-basin predictors.
relationships.display_finding: At fixed label-noise rates of 10% and 20%, SWAG reduced the peak and MultiSWAG eliminated it.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: SWAG and MultiSWAG under 10%/20% label noise
source_check.reason: Peak reduction under SWAG and removal under MultiSWAG in r5, r6, r8 and r9 are consistent with V6's dependence account. V6 does not predict that fixed label noise forces a peak regardless of averaging; these results therefore provide no contrary condition. Multiple peaks and optimal regularization are untested here.
